scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8877: Since a firewall change window this morning, BOTH pods
have lost access to every 10.200.0.x server: DNS queries to 10.200.0.2 time
out and no portal loads by name or by IP. Pod-to-pod traffic between
host_1_1_1_1 and host_2_1_1_1 still works. Monitoring shows all OSPF
adjacencies Full and the 10.200.0.0/24 route present on every router.
Identify what is blocking the server farm.

injection.action: add a FORWARD DROP rule for all traffic destined to the server farm

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router_core_3 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: router_core_3 is the mandatory transit for the server farm --
  switch_server_access attaches only to router_core_3 (172.16.0.10/31). The
  new rule `-A FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP` silently discards every
  FORWARDED packet destined to the farm, from both pods. Routing is
  genuinely healthy: OSPF hellos are INPUT/OUTPUT traffic on router_core_3
  (not FORWARD), so all adjacencies stay Full and 10.200.0.0/24 remains in
  every table -- the drop happens at the firewall layer after the routing
  decision. Pod-to-pod traffic transits router_core_1<->router_core_2 and
  matches no rule. Note: router_core_3's OWN pings to the farm still succeed
  (locally generated traffic traverses OUTPUT, not FORWARD) -- a useful
  discriminator.
Localization: router_core_3
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule for destination
  10.200.0.0/24 on router_core_3
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP` on router_core_3
scenario.fix_spec:
remove the DROP rule on router_core_3 --
`iptables -D FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP`
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: iptables FORWARD DROP rule / firewall filter, not a routing fault
must-recognize-filter-pattern: recognizes that healthy OSPF plus present routes with silent forwarding loss indicates packet filtering on the transit path
bonus-notes-transit-choke: notes all farm traffic must transit router_core_3 (sole attachment of switch_server_access), which is why both pods are affected

agent.diagnosis_text: A spurious iptables FORWARD chain rule was inserted on router_core_3 during the morning firewall change window. The rule is a blanket DROP matching all protocols from any source to the entire 10.200.0.0/24 server-farm subnet (`iptables -A FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP`). Every packet that a host sends toward the server farm arrives at router_core_3 and is forwarded by the kernel toward eth2 (the link to switch_server_access); before it leaves, netfilter evaluates the FORWARD chain and drops it silently. The 12-packet / 1 008-byte counter on that rule — accumulated from our own diagnostic pings — confirms it is actively exercised. Because the rule lives in the FORWARD chain, traffic *originated by router_core_3 itself* (e.g. our test ping from that device) passes through the OUTPUT chain and is unaffected, which is why router_core_3 can reach dns_server but hosts cannot. Pod-to-pod reachability is unaffected because inter-pod traffic is routed through router_core_1/router_core_2 and never hits this rule. OSPF and the routing table remain correct throughout — this is a pure data-plane firewall fault. The corrective fix is to flush the offending rule on router_core_3: `iptables -D FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP`. Persistence should be verified (e.g. in /etc/iptables/rules.v4 or the startup script) to prevent the rule from reloading on reboot.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly names router_core_3 as the affected device in the diagnosis.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-component: iptables FORWARD DROP rule / firewall filter, not a routing fault
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly attributes the outage to an iptables FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP rule on router_core_3 and distinguishes this from a routing/OSPF failure.

per_axis.axis: must-recognize-filter-pattern: recognizes that healthy OSPF plus present routes with silent forwarding loss indicates packet filtering on the transit path
per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly states OSPF and routes are correct but traffic is silently dropped by an iptables FORWARD rule on the transit router, showing recognition of packet-filtering on the path.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-transit-choke: notes all farm traffic must transit router_core_3 (sole attachment of switch_server_access), which is why both pods are affected
per_axis.rationale: The writeup explicitly states that all host packets for the farm arrive at router_core_3 and are forwarded toward the switch_server_access interface (eth2), explaining why traffic from both pods is dropped there.
Correctly recommends deleting the specific FORWARD DROP rule on router_core_3 and verifying persistence, matching the expected fix.

The log contains direct observations of failed host pings, a successful ping from router_core_3, and an iptables FORWARD rule on router_core_3 with matching destination 10.200.0.0/24 and nonzero packet counters; the agent's conclusions follow from these observations and the other devices were checked and found clean. Minor truncation of some command outputs is present but the essential evidence for the DROP rule and its effect is explicit.
